newsitem.title: USA: Trade would welcome USDA weekly meat export data.
newsitem.headline: Trade would welcome USDA weekly meat export data.

text.p: The U.S. Department of Agriculture's proposal to release weekly export data on beef, pork and poultry sales would be welcomed by most in the U.S. livestock industry, trade sources said.

"I think it would be very valuable to have that information," said Joe Kropf, livestock analyst with Kropf & Love Consulting in Overland Park, Kan. "I think it would be of value to the entire industry."
Seeking public comment, USDA unveiled the export proposal in the Federal Register on Thursday.

Under the plan, meat exporters would have to report weekly sales volume, country destination and marketing year for all shipments or face a fine that tops out at $25,000. Such a report would be similar to USDA's existing weekly export report for grains.
Karl Johnson, chairman of the National Pork Producers Council's trade committee, said his group had lobbied USDA to release weekly export data and he hoped that the industry would cooperate fully.
"It's been something that the grain industry has been doing for years and we see it as being workable in the meat industry," Johnson said.
Currently meat export data from USDA is updated monthly, but there is a one- to two-month lag between the time that business is completed and the information is dispersed, livestock analysts said.
Because U.S. meat exports are growing and capturing a larger share of domestic production, more timely export data is needed, analysts and traders said.

In the mid 1980s, exports were less than two percent of annual U.S. beef and pork production, but in 1996 exports are forecast to account for eight percent of beef production and six percent of pork production, according to USDA statistics.
The value of all U.S. red meat exports was $6 billion in 1995, USDA said.

Some worry that packers and exporters will balk at the idea of having to report export sales on a weekly basis, while others said that packers would likely comply because they would benefit by gaining access to information from their competitors.
"Even packers need to know in total what's going on," Kropf said.

A spokesman for Cargill Inc in Minneapolis, Minn. said his company was "in favor of more timely export information," but he declined to comment specifically on the USDA proposal. Cargill is the parent company of the Excel meatpacking concern.
